title: Engines and humans 2: what engines see and what they miss
outcomes: States which of win, draw or hard to hold a fortress position is, using the bishop's colour and the pawn's file, and checks it with a tablebase
Explains why a shallow search can rate a drawn fortress above zero, and asks for a second depth before trusting a number
Reads an engine score on a scale and says what it does and does not show about a pawn sacrifice
Counts the only-moves a defender needs and says why an equal score can still be hard to hold
Writes three questions to ask before believing an engine number

steps.prompt: Your verdict (win, draw or loss) and how sure you are, before any evidence.

steps.text: **The question.** An engine's number feels like a fact. This lesson asks when it misleads a person: a *fortress* that a short search does not see, a *horizon* that hides the truth, a defence with many *only-moves*, and sacrifices whose worth no count shows. By the end you can say win, draw or hard to hold, and explain why the number alone could not tell you.

**An honest wrinkle [V].** The next board is a different case. There the engine does not show a big number, and its score rises with depth: +0.01, +0.15, +0.35 and +1.09 at depths 4, 8, 16 and 30, while the tablebase says draw. So a draw can hide behind a small or rising score as well as a big one.

steps.text: **Two words.** A *rook pawn* stands on the edge file (a or h). A *wrong-coloured bishop* travels on squares whose colour differs from the pawn's promotion corner. Here the corner a8 is light and this bishop is dark, so it can never cover the corner.

**The condition [S].** With a rook pawn and a wrong-coloured bishop, the defender draws if the king reaches the corner. Textbook geometry [S]. The same pieces with Black's king far away, on h8, are a tablebase win [V]. So the file of the pawn, the bishop's colour and where the defending king stands all matter.

steps.text: **Why a b-pawn wins [I].** It promotes on b8, a dark square, and this bishop is dark-squared, so the bishop can guard the queening square while the king cannot hold the corner. The tablebase agrees [V]. A rook pawn has only one neighbouring file, which is what lets the defender hide.

steps.text: **A testable checklist [I].** A *fortress* is a position the stronger side cannot break however long it tries. Ask three questions. (1) Can a check also attack a second piece? If so, no fortress (the queen boards with the king on f8 and on e8). (2) Is every defending unit guarded by another or out of reach? (3) Does the defender have a safe spare move, or can zugzwang bite (the two pawn boards later)?

steps.text: **Other families [H].** Locked pawn chains can also form fortresses. This course has no tablebase-checked board for them yet, so treat that as an idea to test, not a result.

**What 'depth' counts [R].** In engine settings, depth N means the search looks N half-moves (plies) ahead along its main lines, and good engines look further on promising lines. From here on, 'depth N' always means that setting.

steps.prompt: Why might a shallow search rate this position above zero, while the tablebase says draw?

steps.text: **What the engine does [I].** An engine adds up material and piece activity at the end of its search. To see a draw it must see that every winning try fails, which can take many moves. A tablebase simply stores the answer for positions with few pieces.

**What we found [V].** In the queen-versus-rook fortresses, depth 4 to 8 gave +1 to +1.5 and depth 16 to 20 gave 0.00. In the bishop and rook-pawn position the score rose with depth, from +0.01 at depth 4 to +1.09 at depth 30, while the tablebase says draw. [I] A second depth helps in some families, not all; the tablebase is the check when it applies.

**Horizon effect.** The name comes from computer chess: a search that stops at a fixed depth cannot see what lies beyond it [R]. [I] Our fortress numbers are a related problem, the search stopping before the draw is visible, not the classic horizon effect, which is about delaying an unavoidable loss. Treat every number as 'this engine, this depth'.

steps.prompt: A friend says 'the engine says +0.5, so I am better'. Which two things would you ask before agreeing?

steps.text: **Reading a score honestly [H].** A rough guide many players use, not tested here: 0.0 to +0.5 level, about +1 a small edge, +3 and above often winning. Whether +3 wins depends on the position type: fortress positions can read +3 at shallow depth and be drawn. Always note the engine and the depth.

**From score to chance [I].** 'Win probability' curves turn a score into a chance. One public formula, recalled and not re-checked [R], gives 50 + 50 x (2 / (1 + e^(-0.00368 x score in hundredths)) - 1) per cent. Worked here: +1.00 gives about 59%, +3.00 about 75%. The curve is a model fitted to games, not a fact about your position.

steps.text: **Long-term compensation.** A sacrifice may or may not leave the engine near zero. The next boards test three cases at depth 16 and depth 24: a pawn sacrifice where the engine still shows nearly the full pawn, a second whose number shrinks with depth, and an exchange sacrifice that reads level. The numbers, not our expectations, decide what we say.

steps.text: **Disagreeing with the engine [H].** Where compensation comes from pressure and activity, a human's feel may beat a short search or fall short of a deep one. We do not know how often. Hypothesis: write your own view down before looking, because the disagreement is the lesson. Candidates first, engine second.

**Two outside views, rephrased.** Silman is summarised as saying engine analysis shows what to play but not why [S, secondary summary]. Aagaard is reported to say serious errors often begin when a key candidate move is overlooked [S, a reviewer's account]. Neither source was read in full here.

steps.prompt: Choose a position from your own games where you disagreed with an engine. Write your view first, then the engine's, then one reason you now believe for the gap.

steps.text: **The reverse case.** The engine says 0.00, yet the position is hard for a person. A defender may hold only if they find the single saving move several times in a row. The evaluation, 0.00, hides how narrow the path is. We now count those moves.

steps.text: **What this suggests [H].** In practice, a position with many only-moves is more likely to be lost at club level than its 0.00 suggests, while a position that is theoretically lost but needs the opponent to find many only-moves may score better than the engine's number. We have no data of our own to test this; treat it as a hypothesis to check with your own games.

**Who has the waiting moves? [I]** In the next two boards the pieces are identical and only whose turn it is changes. Even a depth-4 search sees the swing here: +4.6 for White with Black to move, +0.08 with White to move [V]. One tempo flips the result. A fortress that survives only while you can shuffle fails the moment you must break it.

steps.text: **Why the pawn step matters [I].** In the f7 board the only saving rook moves went to g6 and e6, squares the pawn on f7 guards. On f6 the pawn no longer guards them, so the rook has no safe shelter and the queen's checks fork it. The tablebase confirms the loss [V].

steps.prompt: In one sentence: why did moving Black's pawn a single step flip the result?

steps.text: **Common mistakes.** Three to watch. Trusting a plus score in a locked position. Giving up material in a fortress because it feels passive: the shelter needs those pieces where they are. Resigning a drawn game because the number looks big. [H] The last is the costliest, because nobody can punish it; you only lose the chance to learn the position.

**A real model case [H].** We have not yet read and checked a famous game where a misread evaluation or a mistaken resignation decided the result, so none is claimed here. Until that is done, the constructed example below is a teaching device, not history.

steps.text: **Three questions before you believe a number.** (1) Which engine and which depth, and does a second depth agree? (2) Is the position locked, or built on a few precise moves, so counting is the wrong tool? (3) What would a person need to do next, and could they? A number answers none of these. [H] Writing the three answers down is a habit worth building.

steps.text: **Self-check.** Did I say when a big score can mislead (a fortress, a short search)? Did I say when it does not (a score over +3 that a tablebase also agrees with)? Did I give an example a beginner could set up on a board? Did I name one mistake? Nothing here is graded; compare your answer with the lesson, not with a mark.

**Recap.** A big score can hide a fortress, and a small or rising score can hide one too. Bishop colour, the file of the pawn and where the defending king stands decide the corner. A second depth is one check, not a guarantee. Compensation is not in the count. A 0.00 can hide five only-moves. Write your view down before the engine's.
